This analysis leverages two key modeling capabilities at LBNL. The DOPER model (described in Section 2.3.3) is used to determine the optimized charging behavior. Inputs to DOPER include the EV driving demand profile (kWh needed to fuel the car in each time interval), the dynamic price profile, and characteristics about the battery. The model then determines the optimal charging profile for the driver under the given price profile. The driving profiles come from LBNL’s BEAM model14, which is an agent-based simulation of transportation in the San Francisco Bay Area. BEAM includes driving behavior across the San Francisco Bay Area’s 7.4 million residents for one illustrative weekday. For this study, we worked with BEAM analysts to cluster these driving behaviors to have representative driving profiles for a range of daily behaviors. We then run a representative sample of thousands of driving profiles through the DOPER model paired with a range of price profiles. In order to understand the year-round impacts of optimized charging, we run the full year of prices assuming the driver’s daily travel patterns are the same every day. From this analysis, we can observe what the optimal charging behavior looks like across the range of drivers, and what their effective charging cost is for each price profile. This will allow us to better understand the range of outcomes for customers with a diverse set of behaviors and determine what groups of customers (as defined by their driving patterns) might be able to respond to prices, and save money, most significantly. 2.4 Technology cost characterization Understanding the cost of technologies that enable automated price response is key to assessing what end use resources can be cost effectively made flexible, and how different price profiles (and therefore bill savings) impact the willingness for customers to invest in automation technologies. Currently, few commercially available technologies can respond to hourly price signals, though significant investment is being made in developing these technologies and preparing them for market.15 In this study, we leverage the technology database developed for the Phase 4 DR Potential Study in order to capture the costs of more broadly available 14 https://transportation.lbl.gov/beam 15 Example: CEC’s CalFlexHub, calflexhub.lbl.gov 17 technologies that, given time, should be able to include price responsive features at similar price points. The parameters used in this study are summarized in Table 2. In general, we select one enabling technology per end use to represent the type of device that is most likely to have price responsive features in the near-term future. Core cost parameters include fixed (per-site) and variable (per-kW of enabled load) up-front and ongoing costs.
